new_statements.relation_note: Catalog penultimate stress is penultimate stress; Campbell states the same placement explicitly and adds the exception classes (Spanish loans, stress-attracting -tsin, Ataco final stress after penult vowel loss) and the note that stress is predictable/unwritten and that length is clearest under penultimate stress.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the word (affixes included: stress moves with derivation, e.g. másat 'deer' vs masá:tsiŋ 'little deer', p. 25); it is predictable and therefore unwritten except in the rare exceptions.
new_statements.exceptions: Three named classes (p. 14, p. 38, p. 49): (a) certain Spanish loans; (b) the diminutive/reverential suffix -tsin, which 'sometimes attracts stress, even though it may be the final syllable, rather than the penultimate as expected by the regular stress rule' (p. 38, Rule 11 Variation; also p. 49 sec. 3.1.3.8: 'In some words this suffix bears the stress even though it may not be the penultimate syllable'); (c) in the Concepción de Ataco dialect, words that lost a penultimate i or u between stops and semivowels now carry final stress, e.g. kwat 'snake', maltyá 'to bathe' (p. 13: 'the lost vowel would ordinarily bear stress when in penultimate position and consequently stress is shifted to the final vowel'). Campbell calls the exceptions 'very rare'. Vowel length is contrastive and clearest in the stressed (penultimate) syllable (p. 25).
new_statements.identity_note: Campbell's grammar covers the Pipil of El Salvador, principally the Cuisnahuat and Santo Domingo de Guzmán dialects (his two main consultant communities); the penultimate rule is stated for 'all dialects of Pipil' (p. 14), with a dialect-specific deviation in Concepción de Ataco, where loss of penultimate i/u between stops and semivowels yields final stress (pp. 13-14).
